# degen

*two models the data can't tell apart*

<!-- badges: start -->
[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/gcol33/degen/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/gcol33/degen/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml)
[![Codecov test coverage](https://codecov.io/gh/gcol33/degen/graph/badge.svg)](https://app.codecov.io/gh/gcol33/degen)
[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-yellow.svg)](https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)
<!-- badges: end -->

degen checks whether competing statistical models can be distinguished by data, such as an exponential model and a gamma model with its shape fixed at one, and whether the parameters of a single model can be estimated, such as two means that enter the likelihood only through their sum.

Two models are observationally equivalent when they assign the same probability to every possible dataset, so no amount of data separates them. degen compares their log-likelihood surfaces: for parameter values of one model it searches for values of the other that give the same log-likelihood, in both directions, and reports the largest discrepancy against a tolerance. For a single model it computes the Fisher information, the curvature of the log-likelihood, and reads its eigenvalues: an eigenvalue near zero marks a parameter combination the likelihood is flat in. You can then decide which of the competing models your data can support, or reparameterize the model so each parameter is estimable.

degen supports:

- **Any log-likelihood.** [`model_spec()`](https://gillescolling.com/degen/reference/model_spec.html) turns a function of the data and named parameters into a model. Ten distributions are built in (`model_spec_normal()`, `model_spec_gamma()`, `model_spec_poisson()`, `model_spec_weibull()` and others), and `model_spec_from_fit()` takes the specification from a fitted `lm` or `glm`.
- **Pairs and sets of models.** [`compare_surfaces()`](https://gillescolling.com/degen/reference/compare_surfaces.html) tests two models by grid search or optimization, and `equivalence_classes()` groups a list of models into classes of mutually equivalent ones by union-find.
- **Parameter mappings.** `check_exact_equivalence()` tests whether given transformations map the parameters of one model onto the other, and `detect_linear_reparam()` searches for a linear reparameterization.
- **Identifiability.** [`identifiability_check()`](https://gillescolling.com/degen/reference/identifiability_check.html) reports which parameters are not identified and which combinations are, from the eigenvalues of the Fisher information; `profile_likelihood()` and `profile_ci()` give profile curves and the intervals read from them.
- **Stability of a verdict.** `sensitivity_analysis()` repeats a comparison over tolerances and grid sizes, and `bootstrap_equivalence()` and `cross_validate_equivalence()` resample the data.
- **Bayesian models.** `compare_posteriors()` and `extract_samples()` work on draws from [brms](https://paulbuerkner.com/brms/), [rstan](https://mc-stan.org/rstan/) and [rstanarm](https://mc-stan.org/rstanarm/), and `prior_sensitivity()` checks how much a prior contributes to identifying a parameter.

A comparison that finds no discrepancy above the tolerance is evidence of equivalence over the points tested, not a proof, and the verdict depends on the tolerance and the number of points. [Comparing Models](https://gillescolling.com/degen/articles/comparing-models.html) shows how both change it.

## Installation

degen is not on CRAN yet. It compiles C++ code, so install the build tools for your operating system first:

| Operating system | Build tools |
|---|---|
| Windows | [Rtools](https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/Rtools/) matching your R version |
| macOS | Run `xcode-select --install` in Terminal |
| Debian / Ubuntu | Install `r-base-dev` |

Check that R can find the compiler:

```r
pkgbuild::has_build_tools(debug = TRUE)
```

Then install degen from GitHub:

```r
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("gcol33/degen")
```

degen needs no system libraries beyond the compiler. Its C++ code links only to Rcpp, which is installed from CRAN with the package.

## Usage

1. Define each model with `model_spec()` or a built-in such as `model_spec_exponential()`.
2. Test two models for equivalence with `equivalence_pair()` and `compare_surfaces()`.
3. Check the parameters of one model with `identifiability_check()`.

A model specification holds a log-likelihood function whose first argument is the data `y` and whose other arguments are the parameters, named in `par_names`, with optional bounds. The data is a numeric vector, or whatever the log-likelihood function accepts.

```{r compare}
library(degen)

set.seed(1)
y <- rexp(200, rate = 2)

exp_model <- model_spec_exponential()
gamma_model <- model_spec_gamma(par = "rate", known_shape = 1)
pair <- equivalence_pair(exp_model, gamma_model)

compare_surfaces(pair, y, tol = 1e-4)
```

A gamma distribution with shape one is the exponential distribution, so the largest discrepancy over the 200 points tested stays below the tolerance. With the default tolerance of `1e-6` the discrepancy of the numerical search, about `7e-6`, would exceed it.

The second model below has two means that enter the likelihood only through their sum:

```{r identify}
sum_model <- model_spec(
  loglik_fn = function(y, a, b) {
    sum(dnorm(y, mean = a + b, sd = 1, log = TRUE))
  },
  par_names = c("a", "b")
)

y2 <- rnorm(100, mean = 5)
identifiability_check(sum_model, y2, par = c(a = 2, b = 3))
```

Neither parameter is identified on its own; their sum is.

## Comparing several models

`equivalence_classes()` compares every pair in a list of models and groups them into classes of equivalent models:

```r
gamma2_model <- model_spec_gamma(par = "rate", known_shape = 2)
models <- list(exponential = exp_model, gamma1 = gamma_model,
               gamma2 = gamma2_model)
equivalence_classes(models, y, tol = 1e-4)
```

`compare_all_pairs()` returns the full matrix of pairwise comparisons, and `find_equivalent_to()` lists the models equivalent to one of them. [Case Studies](https://gillescolling.com/degen/articles/case-studies.html) applies this to competing ecological models of population counts.

## Models from fits and Bayesian draws

`model_spec_from_fit()` takes the specification from a fitted `lm` or `glm`, so an existing model can be checked without writing its log-likelihood. For Bayesian models, `compare_posteriors()` compares two models on their posterior draws. Results export to JSON, CSV or Markdown with `export_results()` and to a LaTeX table with `to_latex()`.

## Documentation

Start with [Introduction to degen](https://gillescolling.com/degen/articles/introduction.html): observational equivalence and identifiability, with a first comparison, an identifiability check and equivalence classes.

- [Writing Model Specifications](https://gillescolling.com/degen/articles/model-specification.html): log-likelihood functions, parameter bounds, validation and common mistakes.
- [Comparing Models](https://gillescolling.com/degen/articles/comparing-models.html): grid and optimization search, tolerances, equivalence classes and plots of the likelihood surface.
- [Identifiability Diagnostics](https://gillescolling.com/degen/articles/identifiability-diagnostics.html): Fisher information, null directions and profile likelihoods.
- [Case Studies](https://gillescolling.com/degen/articles/case-studies.html): competing models applied to example data.
- [Full reference](https://gillescolling.com/degen/reference/): every function.

## Getting help

Questions and bug reports go to the [GitHub issues](https://github.com/gcol33/degen/issues). A bug report is easiest to act on with a small reproducible example, for instance made with [reprex](https://reprex.tidyverse.org/).
